newsitem.title: USA: New York tax credits make clean fuels economical.
newsitem.headline: New York tax credits make clean fuels economical.

text.p: New York tax credits for alternative fuels will provide economic benefits for buyers of vehicles using clean fuels, according to Brooklyn Union Gas Co's director of product and service management.

Noting purchase of these vehicles has been subsidized by the state's utilities "up to now," Chris Cavenagh told Reuters tax legislation the state Legislature passed Monday provides "a whole class (of customers) with economic benefits."
The clan fuels credit covers vehicles powered by natural gas, LPGs, hydrogen and electricity, Assembly Energy Committee spokesman Paul Larrabee said.
Also included, Larrabee said, are those using fuels containing 85 percent methanol, ethanol or other alcohols.
The legislation now awaiting Governor George Pataki's signature calls for tax credits of up to $5,000 each for the purchase of light vehicles using alternate fuels, he said.
And for larger vehicles -- busses and trucks over 14,000 pounds gross weight -- the credit can be as much as $10,000, he added.
Larrabee said the alternative fuels credit is detailed in Section 187B of Assembly Bill 8671 (on page 64).

He pointed out the legislation provides individules and companies other than utilities with tax credits for the purchase of vehicles using alternative fuels. It does not provide credits for modification of existing vehicles.

For vehicles powered by electricity, the credit is 50 percent of the incremental cost of the vehicle -- that is of the difference between its cost and the cost of a similar gasoline powered car of light truck.
For those using clean fuels, the credit is 60 percent of the incremental cost and 50 percent of the cost of purchasing the equipment needed to dispense the fuel.
Calling this "enabling," Cavanagh pointed out the "obstacle has been the higher up front cost" of vehicles using alternate fuels.
He said utilities expect "a whole bunch of new customers will be enabled by this" legislation.
Brooklyn Union has "everything in place we need to capitalize on (the new law)," Cavanagh said.
